claim: Voted for the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act
summary: Hickenlooper's office says he voted to pass the bill and to advance the negotiated version. CBS reported Senate approval 85–5. Coverage describes the bill as cutting red tape and administrative barriers to housing construction. Secondary sources disagree on dates and on final enactment details.
source: Office of Sen. Hickenlooper (corroborated by CBS News)
interpretation: A vote for a bipartisan bill aimed at regulatory barriers to supply. One of 85 yes votes, so it shows alignment more than leadership.

claim: Co-led the bipartisan ePermit Act
summary: Introduced February 2026; would replace paper applications and siloed federal permitting with an interactive online platform.
interpretation: Process reform that could shorten review timelines. Introduction only; no enactment found.

claim: Member of the G-22 bipartisan group that wrote the 2021 infrastructure law
summary: One of 22 senators who negotiated the ~$1.2T Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act; it passed the Senate 69–30 in August 2021 with 19 Republican votes. His office says it included his RECHARGE Act.
interpretation: Direct infrastructure funding and bipartisan negotiation. Spending is not the same as faster building, but the law did fund physical capacity.

claim: Sponsored the BIG WIRES Act (S. 2827)
summary: Would require each FERC planning region to be able to transfer a set share of peak load to neighbors (the lesser of 30% of peak load or peak transmission plus 15%). A Columbia CGEP analysis estimated it would more than double interregional transfer capacity to 191 GW in ten years.
interpretation: Targets a real constraint: transmission is a bottleneck for every kind of generation. Introduced, not enacted.

claim: Says much of the 2026 Senate permitting deal began as his transmission bill
summary: S. 5653 (introduced Sept. 30, 2026 by Capito, Lee, Whitehouse, Heinrich) revises NEPA, CWA and ESA processes and gives FERC permitting authority for transmission in the public interest. Hickenlooper is not a sponsor. A floor vote is expected after the election. No public statement of how he will vote was found.
legislation: S. 5653, Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026
interpretation: His claim of influence is plausible given BIG WIRES, but his actual vote is not yet known. It is the most important pending test of his permitting stance.

claim: Co-led the Geo POWER Act with Sen. Daines; passed Energy committee
summary: Introduced March 17, 2026. Gives DOE financing tools and milestone-based investments for next-generation geothermal demonstrations; his office describes about $800M. Passed the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee as amended.
source: Office of Sen. Hickenlooper; GovInfo S. 4116
interpretation: Supports firm, around-the-clock clean power. Public money for demonstrations is a subsidy, but aimed at new supply.

claim: Voted against advancing the Ratepayer Protection Act
summary: After the House passed it 417–3, the bill failed Senate cloture 57–43. Hickenlooper voted no, calling it inadequate: it asks states to consider ratepayer protections but does not require them. He argues data centers should pay grid costs and meet local water and noise standards.
source: Office of Sen. Hickenlooper; CBS News
interpretation: Contrary evidence on its face, since he blocked a near-unanimous House bill. His stated reason is cost allocation, not limiting supply, but adding local standards could slow data-center buildout.

claim: As governor, brokered methane rules and a 2014 deal that kept anti-fracking measures off the ballot
summary: In 2013–14 Colorado became the first state to limit methane from oil and gas production, under rules written jointly by producers and the Environmental Defense Fund. In August 2014 he brokered a deal that withdrew four ballot measures and set up a task force.
interpretation: Executive record of keeping gas supply going while adding environmental rules. Shows a willingness to break with his party's left on energy.

claim: Voted for the ADVANCE Act (advanced-reactor licensing reform)
summary: The Senate concurred in the House amendments to S. 870, which carried the ADVANCE Act, 88–2 on June 18, 2024 (Vote No. 200). The Senate floor log lists the only nays (Markey, Sanders) and all ten non-voters (Braun, Cramer, Durbin, Fetterman, Hoeven, Marshall, Menendez, Sinema, Sullivan, Tuberville). Hickenlooper is in neither list, so he voted yes. No bill he sponsored or co-sponsored on fission was found.
source: U.S. Senate Periodical Press Gallery floor log (corroborated by ANS)
interpretation: A yes vote on the main recent law to speed NRC licensing of advanced reactors. One of 88 votes, so it shows alignment rather than leadership on nuclear.

claim: Voted for the Inflation Reduction Act
summary: The IRA passed the Senate 51–50 in August 2022 with all Democrats voting yes. It created long-term tax credits for wind, solar, storage, nuclear and other generation.
interpretation: Subsidies that expanded generation supply. Party-line vote, so it says little about independence.

claim: CHIPS and Science Act conferee and science-subcommittee chair
summary: As chair of the Commerce Committee's Space and Science Subcommittee he oversaw NSF, NIST, NASA and OSTP. He sat on the conference committee and presided over the final Senate vote. The law includes semiconductor incentives and advanced-nuclear R&D provisions.
source: Office of Sen. Hickenlooper; Congress.gov H.R. 4346
interpretation: Strong evidence of support for research and domestic manufacturing.

claim: Co-led the VET AI Act with Sen. Capito
summary: S. 2615 directs NIST to develop voluntary specifications for third-party evaluators who verify AI developers' testing and risk-management claims. Reintroduced July 31, 2025.
interpretation: Voluntary standards are light-touch and could build trust that helps adoption.

claim: Wants third-party AI evaluators, developer liability for damages, and data-privacy protections
summary: Colorado Sun candidate guide: he would like third-party evaluators overseeing AI work, assurances that developers can be sued for damages their products cause, and protections for private data.
interpretation: Liability and oversight have intended consumer benefits but raise deployment costs and legal uncertainty, especially for smaller developers.

claim: Opposed a 10-year federal moratorium on state AI laws; wants Congress to set national standards
summary: His office predicted the moratorium would be stripped from H.R. 1. The Senate struck it 99–1 on July 1, 2025 (Blackburn amendment). Only Sen. Tillis voted no, which implies Hickenlooper voted to strip it.
interpretation: Keeps states able to regulate AI, a patchwork that raises compliance costs, while saying he prefers federal standards. His vote is inferred from the 99–1 tally.

claim: Passed a bipartisan quantum development investment bill through Commerce Committee
summary: His office reports Commerce Committee passage of a bipartisan quantum investment bill. The bill number and date were not captured in the sources found.
interpretation: Supports research funding. Committee stage only.

claim: Voted to terminate the national emergency used for tariffs on Canada
summary: Senate roll call 160 (April 2, 2025), S.J.Res. 37; Hickenlooper voted Yea. Four Republicans joined Democrats.
interpretation: Supports trade openness and lower input costs.

claim: Voted to end 50% tariffs on Brazil
summary: His office says he voted with all Democrats and five Republicans to end the Brazil tariffs.
legislation: Joint resolution on Brazil tariff emergency
interpretation: Consistent with H16.

claim: Voted against the 2025 reconciliation law (H.R. 1)
summary: H.R. 1 passed the Senate 51–50 on July 1, 2025 with every Democrat opposed. It made full expensing for equipment and domestic R&D permanent, cut Medicaid, and phased out wind and solar credits.
legislation: H.R. 1 (119th), One Big Beautiful Bill Act
interpretation: Counter-evidence on investment incentives (expensing), though his no vote also reflected the bill's energy-credit and health cuts. A large omnibus vote is a weak signal on any one issue.

claim: Ranked 27th of 98 senators on the Lugar Center Bipartisan Index (2023); 62nd in 2021
summary: The index measures how often a member's bills attract cosponsors from the other party and how often they cosponsor the other party's bills. 2023 score 0.41157.
interpretation: Above the Senate median recently. Measures cosponsorship, not votes or results.

claim: Governor 2011–2019; Denver mayor 2003–2011; founded a brewpub business
summary: Long executive record at city and state level before entering the Senate in 2021.
interpretation: Extensive administrative experience. Not by itself proof of policy alignment.

claim: Says he now regrets voting to confirm Trump Cabinet nominees
summary: In the Oct. 14, 2026 9NEWS debate he said his earlier strategy of supporting some nominees to 'reduce the damage' for Colorado did not work.
interpretation: Shows he once broke with his party on confirmations, and that he now says he would not.

claim: Won the Democratic primary 52.8% over progressive state Sen. Julie Gonzales
summary: A narrow primary win against a challenger from his party's left.
interpretation: Context: he is positioned toward the center of his party.

claim: Co-founded CAI (Commissioning Agents, Inc.) in 1996; CEO until 2022
summary: CAI serves life-sciences, data-center and industrial manufacturers. The succession announcement credits him with growing it to a $135M global firm with 750 employees. He stayed on as board chair and chief innovation officer. Campaign coverage calls it employee-owned; that detail was not independently confirmed.
interpretation: Real record of building and running a technical firm. Relevant to execution; not proof of policy skill.

claim: Navy submarine officer with a nuclear engineering background
summary: CPR reports he has a nuclear engineering background from Navy service.
interpretation: Relevant context for nuclear policy, but no explicit nuclear policy found.

claim: Former Republican; switched to the Forward Party in 2025
summary: CPR's voter guide identifies him as the Forward Party nominee. He calls his campaign independent. He says the Forward Party has no policy positions.
interpretation: Ballot status confirmed. Party switch is recent.

claim: Calls the housing shortage a supply-and-demand problem worsened by regulation that delays building
summary: His issues page lists mortgage rates, construction costs and government regulation that delays building more homes as causes.
interpretation: Correct supply-side diagnosis, with no specific mechanism.

claim: Blames tariffs and regulations for higher home-building costs; ties the national debt to mortgage rates
summary: In CPR's voter guide he attributed most affordability problems to government actions such as tariffs and regulations that raise building costs, and said he has a 'credible plan' on the debt.
interpretation: Points to input costs and capital costs, both supply-side.

claim: Says data-center demand cannot be met by wind and solar alone; backs an all-of-the-above strategy
summary: His issues page says demand from data centers, cloud servers and AI queries 'cannot possibly be met by wind and solar alone' and calls for an all-of-the-above strategy. See C20 for the nuclear part of the same page.
interpretation: Technology-neutral, supply-focused framing. No mechanism given.

claim: Calls for a 'more measured' renewable transition; cites gas at roughly half of coal's CO2
summary: In the CPR interview he also said Colorado pays the highest retail electricity rates of its neighboring states.
interpretation: Weighs reliability and cost. Mostly about Colorado policy, with less federal detail.

claim: Lists restoring American energy dominance among his goals
summary: Reported in the Colorado Newsline voter guide citing his website.
interpretation: Slogan-level.

claim: No technology platform found; AI mentioned only as a health-care cost tool
summary: In the CPR interview he listed price transparency, competition and greater use of technology, 'including that dreaded word AI', as parts of health-care cost reform.
interpretation: Mildly positive toward deployment, but not enough to score.

claim: 'Tariffs are a tax, plain and simple'; wants Congress to reassert tariff authority
summary: His site says tariffs raise consumer prices, create uncertainty for small businesses, and punish domestic exporters.
interpretation: Clear pro-trade position with a constitutional-process element.

claim: Would let each state decide how many visas it accepts in each category
summary: Confirmed in the CPR interview and described in CPR's voter guide.
interpretation: New idea. It could raise skilled admissions in states that want talent, or lower them elsewhere. Net effect is uncertain.

claim: Close capital-gains and estate-tax loopholes for the ultra-wealthy; earmark revenue for debt reduction and entitlement solvency
summary: His top issue is the national debt (more than $40 trillion), which he calls 'a ticking time bomb.'
interpretation: Higher tax on inherited capital, against lower fiscal risk and interest rates. The capital-formation effect depends on design.

claim: Focus enforcement on violent criminals and cartel traffickers, not peaceful immigrants who contribute to the economy
summary: Stated on his campaign site.
interpretation: Labor-supply friendly.

claim: Would not support reconciliation bills; calls bipartisanship the best long-term approach
summary: Stated in CPR's voter guide.
interpretation: A pro-consensus pledge. It would also rule out the main way recent Congresses have passed tax and energy law, which could limit what he can deliver.

claim: Largely self-funded (more than $1M of his own money; $1.5M ad expansion); excluded from 9NEWS debate
summary: Colorado Politics reports the self-funding and ad buys. He did not meet 9NEWS's 15% polling threshold. A Substack interview says he was not allowed to take part in the Club 20 debate.
interpretation: Context on viability. It does not measure governing ability.

claim: Hickenlooper campaign: he donated heavily to GOP senators including Susan Collins. Chew: he gave to moderates of both parties
summary: Both claims come from the campaigns. The FEC donation record was not checked independently for this analysis.
interpretation: Checked against FEC records in C22: both statements are partly true.

claim: Supports open primaries and ranked-choice voting
summary: Reported by Smarter.vote and IVN as part of his platform.
interpretation: Reforms meant to reduce partisan incentives.

claim: Criticized President Trump's handling of the war in Iran despite his Republican past
summary: Reported by CPR.
interpretation: Breaks with his former party on a major issue.

claim: Says the Forward Party has no policy positions
summary: Said in the CPR interview.
interpretation: His positions are his own. There is no party caucus or platform to lean on.

claim: Voted NO on HB24-1313 (Housing in Transit-Oriented Communities)
summary: Official Senate third-reading record, May 7, 2024: passed 19–15, Baisley No. The bill set housing-capacity goals near transit for larger cities.
interpretation: A vote against the state's main density-near-transit supply bill. It may reflect a local-control principle, but the effect on supply is negative.

claim: Voted NO on HB24-1152 (Accessory Dwelling Units)
summary: Official Senate third-reading record, May 6, 2024: passed 20–15, Baisley No. He voted yes on a same-day amendment that passed 35–0.
interpretation: ADU legalization is one of the most direct supply reforms available. Voting no runs against the stated objective.

claim: Voted YES on SB24-174 (statewide housing-needs assessment)
summary: Passed the Senate 32–1 on April 19, 2024 and the concurrence 35–0, with Baisley voting yes. It requires a statewide needs assessment and local grants.
interpretation: A study and planning bill. It does not change rules that limit building.

claim: Cites NAHB: regulatory costs up ~40% in five years, adding ~$131,734 to a new home; blames 'unelected bureaucrats'
summary: Reported by The Center Square from his campaign materials.
interpretation: Supply-side diagnosis aimed at federal rules. It sits in tension with his state votes on zoning.

claim: Proposes tax breaks for lenders tied to the 10-year Treasury yield to lower mortgage rates
summary: Stated in CPR's voter guide, along with a national fix for property taxes.
interpretation: Subsidizes demand. Without more supply, cheaper credit tends to push prices up.

claim: Prime sponsor of SB25-139, which would have counted nuclear as a clean energy resource
summary: Introduced Feb. 5, 2025; postponed indefinitely by the Senate State, Veterans & Military Affairs Committee on March 4, 2025.
interpretation: Concrete pro-nuclear effort. It did not pass.

claim: Pursued legislation to restore uranium mining in western Colorado (unsuccessful)
summary: Highlighted in the Colorado Sun candidate guide, which says he pushed unsuccessfully for state legislation to let uranium mining return to western Colorado as part of a broader nuclear push. A search of legislature records did not identify the bill number.
interpretation: Fuel-supply side of nuclear. Unverified at the bill level.

claim: Would keep using carbon-emitting sources; sees natural gas meeting AI-driven demand; backs government research on hydrogen and nuclear
summary: From CPR's voter guide and the Colorado Sun candidate guide. He also says he supports efforts to minimize human impact on the climate.
source: Colorado Public Radio voter guide; The Colorado Sun
interpretation: Favors firm supply. Less clear on renewables, storage and transmission.

claim: Pledges 'American energy dominance', energy independence, and regulatory rollback
summary: Campaign pledge reported by Colorado Politics and Colorado Newsline.
interpretation: Slogan-level.

claim: Supports the 2025 reconciliation law (H.R. 1)
summary: CPR reports he supports both the GOP spending bill and Trump's tariffs. H.R. 1 phased out wind and solar credits and made full expensing permanent.
interpretation: Fewer subsidies may slow near-term wind and solar buildout, while expensing helps capital investment.

claim: Voted YES on final concurrence of the Colorado AI Act (SB24-205)
summary: Official record, May 8, 2024: 35–0, Baisley Yes. One aggregator lists him as a primary sponsor; the official sponsor list names Rodriguez, Titone and Rutinel.
interpretation: He supported the nation's first broad state AI-discrimination law, which industry widely criticized as burdensome. Counter-evidence to his 'regulate lightly' stance.

claim: Lead Senate sponsor of SB25B-004, delaying the AI Act to June 30, 2026
summary: Signed Aug. 28, 2025 in a special session. In May 2026 the legislature repealed and replaced the Act with a disclosure-based framework.
interpretation: Reduced near-term compliance burden on AI deployers.

claim: Co-sponsored HB24-1058 adding neural and biological data to the Colorado Privacy Act
summary: Bipartisan sponsors: Reps. Kipp and Soper; Sens. Priola and Baisley. Signed by Gov. Polis.
interpretation: A narrow privacy rule for neurotech. Modest compliance cost; also shows bipartisan work.

claim: Says AI should be regulated 'lightly', mainly by applying existing laws, with protections against discrimination and deepfakes
summary: Colorado Sun candidate guide and debate coverage.
interpretation: Deployment-friendly stance.

claim: Calls the Space Command move to Alabama political; would fight for aerospace jobs
summary: Said in the CPR interview. He also blamed Hickenlooper for not keeping Space Command in Colorado.
interpretation: Supports the aerospace sector. Also a rare break with the Trump administration.

claim: Senate sponsor of HB25-1157, reauthorizing Colorado's Advanced Industries tax credit
summary: Co-sponsored with Democratic Sen. Snyder; signed by the governor.
interpretation: Supports investment in advanced industries, including aerospace, bioscience and cleantech.

claim: Defends Trump's tariffs; wants tariff revenue to eventually replace the federal income tax
summary: Said in the CPR interview.
interpretation: Replacing income-tax revenue would require very high, broad tariffs, raising input costs and inviting retaliation against exporters.

claim: Deport dangerous immigrants; vetted legal immigrants can stay; ~1M legal admissions a year is small enough to assimilate
summary: CPR voter guide.
interpretation: Accepts current legal levels. No position found on skilled-visa expansion.

claim: Co-sponsored HB21-1230 (agency rulemaking search) with Democrat Brianna Titone; 98 of 100 legislators supported it
summary: Signed in July 2021. Baisley said people with different social views can readily agree on technical problems.
interpretation: Practical, transparency-minded lawmaking across party lines.

claim: 2026 session: prime sponsor of 12 bills, 5 signed into law
summary: The legislature's member page for the 2026 regular session lists 12 bills with Baisley as prime sponsor. Five were signed: SB26-186 (electronic filing for workers' compensation), SB26-185 (state IT security), HB26-1238 (EMS as essential services), HB26-1205 (State Forest Service Good Neighbor Authority) and HB26-1023 (party liability for accessibility). Five were postponed indefinitely and two were pending. None concerned energy or housing. An earlier aggregator count of 4 enacted bills over his career could not be reconciled with this and is not used.
interpretation: A 5-of-12 rate in a Democratic-controlled legislature shows he can pass technical, low-salience bills. None are on the abundance agenda's core issues.

claim: Featured speaker at an April 2022 Capitol rally with Mike Lindell and Tina Peters
summary: Reported by States Newsroom. In the Oct. 14, 2026 9NEWS debate, moderator Kyle Clark pressed him on his past embrace of election-rigging claims.
interpretation: Evidence of ideological rigidity. Damages cross-party trust.

claim: Said he made a mistake supporting GOP amendments endorsing election-fraud claims
summary: In early 2022 he told a radio interviewer his votes for those House amendments were a mistake.
interpretation: A partial walk-back, followed months later by the rally appearance (B21).

claim: 2025 laws co-sponsored with Democrats: HB25-1195 (with Mullica) and HB25-1053 (with Marchman)
summary: HB25-1195: first-responder voter-record confidentiality. HB25-1053: landowner immunity for emergency access. Both signed.
interpretation: Steady cross-party work on narrow bills.

claim: 40-year IT career in aerospace and defense (NASA, Hughes, Raytheon, Martin Marietta); founding board president of STEM School and Academy; former Colorado GOP vice chair
summary: From his Senate Republicans biography and Ballotpedia.
interpretation: Relevant technical background. Not proof of policy alignment.

claim: Called Hickenlooper's criticism 'TDS'; said Americans will 'all have to pay a little bit more' for fuel because of the Iran war
summary: Coverage of the Oct. 14, 2026 9NEWS debate.
interpretation: Stands with the President on a policy that raises energy costs.

claim: Describes himself as building coalitions while voting contrarian
summary: Colorado Politics Q&A.
interpretation: Self-assessment.

claim: Expects natural gas to be needed to meet AI-driven demand; names geothermal and fusion as promising; opposes federal preemption of local data-center decisions
summary: In the Colorado Sun candidate guide he backs a transition to clean energy by 2050, says natural gas will be needed in the meantime to meet growing demand from AI, and names geothermal and fusion as promising. On data centers he said he is not in favor of the federal government taking siting decisions away from localities.
interpretation: Pragmatic on gas as a bridge, which supports near-term supply. Keeping data-center siting local preserves a veto point that can slow large loads and the generation built for them.

claim: Supports guest-worker visas for working taxpayers and a citizenship pathway for DACA recipients
summary: In the Colorado Sun guide he says legal pathways are being 'dismantled and in many cases ignored' and backs guest-worker visas and a DACA pathway. No current skilled-immigration (H-1B, STEM green card) bill of his was found.
interpretation: Favors a larger legal labor supply. Not specific to high-skill talent, which matters most for the technology category.

claim: Backs an all-of-the-above strategy with 'a heavy reliance on nuclear power' and investment in small modular reactors
summary: His campaign issues page calls for reliable, abundant energy with heavy reliance on nuclear and investment in small modular reactors. It gives no position on NRC licensing, fuel supply, transmission or natural gas permitting.
interpretation: Supply-focused and specific on technology, but no mechanism (licensing, financing, siting) is given. Consistent with his Navy nuclear background, which is context, not proof.

claim: Housing plan: 'tame our national deficits, reduce tariffs, welcome immigration labor, and repeal costly regulations'
summary: His issues page says 'overbearing environmental regulations and permit processes' delay construction, and names tariffs, inflation and immigration enforcement as raising building costs. It names no specific regulation, permitting reform or zoning change. In a June 2026 IVN interview he argued a credible debt plan would lower mortgage rates without targeted housing legislation.
source: Bob Chew campaign website (with IVN interview, 2026-06-17)
interpretation: Mostly supply-side levers (labor, materials costs, regulation). The debt-to-mortgage-rate channel is indirect and works on demand-side cost of credit; no concrete supply mechanism.

claim: FEC records: gave to Republicans, Democrats and independents; more to Republicans overall, more to Democrats and independents since joining Forward
summary: Itemized FEC receipts for 'Chew, Robert' of Boulder, CO (employer CAI / R Chew LLC), Oct 2020–Oct 2026, excluding his own campaign and ActBlue/WinRed conduit lines: about $92K to Republican committees (e.g., Todd Young, Lawler, Hogan, Bacon, Murkowski, Collins, NRSC), $59K to Democrats (e.g., Manchin, Golden, Gottheimer), $36K to independent candidates, and $57K to PACs including No Labels, the Forward Party and United Independents. Since his first Forward Party gift (Sept. 2025): about $22K to Democrats, $32K to independents, $13K to Republicans, including $5.5K to Sen. Collins and $940 to Sen. Cassidy.
interpretation: Confirms the Hickenlooper campaign's claim of heavy GOP giving before 2025 and Chew's claim of giving to moderates in both parties. The pattern favors centrist and independent candidates over either party's base. Name match is consistent across 154 records but was not confirmed with the campaign.

claim: Plans to work with a bloc of independent senators as a 'fulcrum'; wants budgets through regular order, reconciliation narrowed, and a 60-vote threshold restored for confirmations
summary: In a June 2026 IVN interview he described a planned group of independent Senate candidates who would deny either party an automatic majority and publish joint non-negotiables. He said passing budgets is 'job number one for the legislative branch'.
interpretation: A concrete theory of how an unaffiliated senator would get leverage. Whether it works depends on how many independents win and on the Senate margin, which is outside his control.

claim: Senate sponsor of HB25-1040, which made nuclear a 'clean energy resource' under Colorado law; signed March 31, 2025
summary: The legislature's bill page lists Sens. Liston and Roberts as Senate prime sponsors and Baisley as an additional sponsor. The bill counts nuclear toward utilities' 2050 clean-energy target and makes it eligible for local clean-energy financing. It became law (Session Law Ch. 45, effective Aug. 6, 2025). It followed his own SB25-139 and the 2023 SB23-079, which did not pass.
interpretation: Removes a legal barrier to nuclear in Colorado's clean-energy rules. A bipartisan bill he helped carry, not one he led.

claim: Data-center siting is a local decision; data centers should pay for their electricity but not be treated differently from other large users; wants to 'get back on the nuclear track'
summary: In the Colorado Sun guide he said water concerns about data centers are overblown because of closed-loop cooling (the Sun notes not all use it), and that data centers should pay for power like other large customers.
interpretation: Treats large new loads as ordinary customers, which eases their build-out. Like Hickenlooper, he leaves siting to localities.
